title: Hospital switching at first readmission and recurrent hospitalization after heart failure
text:
Hospital switching at a readmission can reflect care transitions, referral, access, patient preference, and clinical routing. The association between switching at a first readmission and a further admission after discharge from that readmission is not necessarily a measure of fragmented care or hospital quality.



To estimate the association between a different versus same hospital for the first all-cause readmission after an eligible heart-failure (HF) index hospitalization and a second readmission, defined as any inpatient admission within 30 days after the first-readmission discharge.



This retrospective cohort study uses the 2016–2022 HCUP Nationwide Readmissions Database (NRD). Adults with an eligible principal-diagnosis HF hospitalization in January through October were followed to a first all-cause readmission within 30 days; HF diagnosis at that first readmission was not required for cohort entry. The analytic population is further restricted to people recorded as alive at discharge from that readmission. The outcome, termed the second readmission, is any inpatient admission within 30 days after the first-readmission discharge. The target is the survey-weighted conditional association among people reaching this survivor cohort. The analysis plan was revised retrospectively before the new outcome models were fit; it was not prespecified before the study.
Among people in the survivor cohort after an all-cause first readmission, the primary analysis used a survey-weighted logistic model with year, sex, payer, ZIP income quartile, county rurality, index-hospital bed size, urban-teaching status and ownership, natural splines for age and log(1 + index length of stay), index discharge disposition, APR-DRG severity, and mapped legacy Elixhauser indicators that were nonconstant and estimable. Standardized risks were estimated with predictive margins. The fitted formula, outcome-blind spline knots, and any structural simplifications are reported in the supplement.



The revised primary model included 502,236 complete cases. The adjusted risk was 31.44% (95% CI 31.26% to 31.61%) after a same-hospital first readmission (n = 394,183), and 32.49% (95% CI 32.18% to 32.80%) after a different-hospital first readmission (n = 108,053). The adjusted risk difference (different minus same hospital) was 1.06 percentage points (95% CI 0.71 to 1.40).



The analysis concerns a selected group who had a first readmission and survived to its discharge. The observed association cannot establish that changing hospitals causes or prevents another admission. NRD does not capture out-of-hospital deaths or readmissions across states or calendar-year boundaries.

title: Hospital fragmentation and second readmission after heart failure
text:
Among adults hospitalized for heart failure whose index and first-readmission discharges are recorded as alive, and whose first readmission occurs within 30 days, is discharge from the same hospital rather than a different hospital associated with another readmission within 30 days?
The study uses US Nationwide Readmissions Database records from 2016-2022. The analysis accounts for the database’s hospital sampling design and uses discharge weights. The results describe an association among people who reached the second stage of this care pathway. They do not estimate what would happen if a hospital changed its referral or transfer practices.

Main findings
The adjusted model estimates a 30-day second-readmission risk of 31.4% (31.3% to 31.6%) for patients whose first readmission was at the same hospital, and 32.5% (32.2% to 32.8%) for those readmitted to a different hospital. The adjusted risk difference (different minus same hospital) was 1.1 percentage points (95% CI 0.7 to 1.4 percentage points). The adjusted risk ratio was 1.034 (95% CI 1.023 to 1.045).
These adjusted values come from the primary model, which includes measured patient and hospital characteristics available in the database. A separate conditional model adds measured characteristics of the first readmission. Both estimates may still reflect differences the data could not measure.

title: Hospital fragmentation and second readmission after heart failure
text:
Methods in brief
The analytic population begins with adults whose principal heart failure hospitalization is recorded as discharged alive from January through October. It then requires a first 30-day readmission recorded as alive at discharge (DIED=0) by November, leaving the full 30-day window observable within that calendar year. The first-readmission flow count precedes the known-alive screen; patients with an in-hospital death or unknown death status are not eligible for the second-stage risk set. Transfers are excluded from the readmission risk set because the hospital attribution or follow-up for the next event is not defined consistently for those discharges. The exposure compares whether that first readmission was to the same hospital as the index stay or to a different hospital. The outcome is any further inpatient readmission within 30 days after the first readmission.
The models account for the NRD’s stratified hospital sampling design and discharge weights. The primary model adjusts for calendar year and measured patient and hospital characteristics. A separate conditional model also adjusts for measured first-readmission characteristics. The analysis uses annual linkage identifiers because NRD patient linkage is limited to each calendar year. See the analysis code and aggregate tables for the full variable definitions and model specification.

title: Hospital fragmentation and second readmission after heart failure
text:
Limitations
This is an observational analysis of administrative discharge records. The primary complete-case model includes 502,236 discharges from 512,770 eligible second-stage discharges; records missing required model covariates are excluded. Differences between patients treated at the same or different hospitals may reflect clinical severity, access to care, referral patterns, or social factors unavailable in the database, leaving residual confounding. Diagnosis codes do not provide the clinical detail of a medical record, and coding may be incomplete. Readmissions outside the NRD’s observable linkage are not captured, including care across state boundaries and events after the annual linkage window. Out-of-hospital deaths are not observed, so some patients classified as at risk may have died before a recorded readmission. Patients who die during a hospitalization cannot experience a subsequent readmission and are outside this conditional prognosis estimand. The results are adjusted associations among survivors who experienced a first readmission, not causal effects of hospital continuity or fragmentation.

title: Hospital switching at first readmission and recurrent hospitalization after heart failure
text:
Hospital switching at a readmission can reflect care transitions, referral, access, patient preference, and clinical routing. The association between switching at a first readmission and a further admission after discharge from that readmission is not necessarily a measure of fragmented care or hospital quality.



To estimate the association between a different versus same hospital for the first all-cause readmission after an eligible heart-failure (HF) index hospitalization and a second readmission, defined as any inpatient admission within 30 days after the first-readmission discharge.



This retrospective cohort study uses the 2016–2022 HCUP Nationwide Readmissions Database (NRD). Adults with an eligible principal-diagnosis HF hospitalization in January through October were followed to a first all-cause readmission within 30 days; HF diagnosis at that first readmission was not required for cohort entry. The analytic population is further restricted to people recorded as alive at discharge from that readmission. The outcome, termed the second readmission, is any inpatient admission within 30 days after the first-readmission discharge. The target is the survey-weighted conditional association among people reaching this survivor cohort. The analysis plan was revised retrospectively before the new outcome models were fit; it was not prespecified before the study.
Among people in the survivor cohort after an all-cause first readmission, the primary analysis used a survey-weighted logistic model with year, sex, payer, ZIP income quartile, county rurality, index-hospital bed size, urban-teaching status and ownership, natural splines for age and log(1 + index length of stay), index discharge disposition, APR-DRG severity, and mapped legacy Elixhauser indicators that were nonconstant and estimable. Standardized risks were estimated with predictive margins. The fitted formula, outcome-blind spline knots, and any structural simplifications are reported in the supplement.



The revised primary model included 502,236 complete cases. The adjusted risk was 31.44% (95% CI 31.26% to 31.61%) after a same-hospital first readmission (n = 394,183), and 32.49% (95% CI 32.18% to 32.80%) after a different-hospital first readmission (n = 108,053). The adjusted risk difference (different minus same hospital) was 1.06 percentage points (95% CI 0.71 to 1.40).



The analysis concerns a selected group who had a first readmission and survived to its discharge. The observed association cannot establish that changing hospitals causes or prevents another admission. NRD does not capture out-of-hospital deaths or readmissions across states or calendar-year boundaries.

title: Hospital switching at first readmission and recurrent hospitalization after heart failure
text:
Introduction
Heart-failure readmissions are common markers of illness burden and care transitions. A readmission to a hospital different from the index hospital may result from patient choice, referral, emergency routing, geography, insurance networks, capacity, or clinical need. The hospital identifier therefore describes site continuity in the discharge data; it does not reveal whether clinicians shared records, whether a transfer was clinically appropriate, or whether care was fragmented.
Prior observational work has compared outcomes during same- versus different-hospital HF readmissions in Canadian and U.S. cohorts (McAlister et al; Lahewala et al). VA research has examined later readmissions after cross-system use (Axon et al), and repeat HF admissions have been described in NRD (Thandra et al). A systematic review identified a small set of studies addressing later or third admissions, with populations and exposure definitions that differ from the present question (Snow et al). More recent NRD work continues to study same- versus different-hospital readmission outcomes (Turbow et al; Verma et al). These studies motivate examining what happens after the first readmission, while leaving important differences in populations, exposure definitions, and follow-up. We therefore avoid a novelty claim and frame the question narrowly: among adults with an eligible HF index admission who are readmitted within 30 days and discharged alive from that first readmission, is a different-hospital first readmission associated with another inpatient admission within the following 30 days?

title: Hospital switching at first readmission and recurrent hospitalization after heart failure
text:
Methods

Design and data source
We conducted a retrospective cohort analysis of the HCUP NRD for 2016–2022. The NRD is a state-based, all-payer inpatient database designed to support within-year linkage of hospital discharges in participating states. Its discharge weights support inference to the NRD target universe for each annual sample, not to every U.S. patient or to longitudinal care across years and states. Patient linkage identifiers, hospital identifiers, and sampling strata are year-specific; admissions after a year boundary and admissions in another state are not linked in this analysis.


Cohort construction
Within each year, we selected adults aged 18 years or older with a principal diagnosis matching the project’s administrative HF phenotype and an index discharge from January through October. The phenotype uses normalized ICD-10-CM principal-diagnosis prefixes I50, I110, I130, I132, or I0981. For each patient-year, the earliest eligible index admission is selected using the source ordering by NRD_DAYSTOEVENT and KEY_NRD. Index discharges with recorded in-hospital death, unavailable linkage or hospital identifiers, or the documented same-day event and transfer restrictions are excluded according to the cohort code.
The cohort flow is ordered by event time. We identify the first all-cause readmission within 30 days after the index discharge before applying the first-readmission discharge-status and follow-up restrictions. To enter the second-stage cohort, the first readmission must be discharged alive (DIED=0), occur early enough to allow 30 days of within-year follow-up, and meet the same-day, rehabilitation-transfer, and acute-transfer disposition rules implemented in the code. The report uses the published coarsened transfer flow and does not reveal private component counts.


Exposure Outcome and Estimand
The exposure is a different-hospital first readmission: the HOSP_NRD identifier for the first readmission differs from that of the HF index admission. The comparator is a first readmission at the same hospital identifier. This operational measure captures hospital-site switching within a year; it does not directly measure provider continuity, shared records, or a health-system relationship.
Follow-up for the primary outcome begins at discharge from the first readmission. The second readmission is any inpatient admission within 30 days. It is not restricted to HF and is not labeled unplanned. Patients are censored by the available within-year follow-up boundary; the data do not identify out-of-hospital death as a competing event.
The estimand is the survey-weighted, covariate-adjusted difference in predicted 30-day admission risks among adults who experienced the eligible index HF hospitalization, had a first all-cause readmission within 30 days, and were recorded alive at discharge from that first readmission. Conditioning on both readmission and survival defines a selected survivor population and may induce selection bias. This is an adjusted association, not a causal effect of hospital switching.


Covariates and statistical analysis
The revised primary model included year, sex, payer, ZIP income quartile, county urban-rural category, index-hospital bed size, index-hospital urban-teaching status and ownership, natural cubic splines for age and log(1 + index length of stay), index discharge disposition, APR-DRG severity category, and all mapped legacy Elixhauser indicators that were nonconstant and estimable. APR-DRG severity code 0 was retained as a category distinct from missingness; no Elixhauser summary count was included with the individual indicators. Spline knots were set at the 5th, 35th, 65th, and 95th percentiles in the primary complete-case population without using the outcome. The final fitted formula, computed knot locations, and any structurally dropped terms are reported from the analysis summary. All adjustment variables refer to the index admission before the first-readmission destination, although claims-based severity and comorbidity flags may include conditions recorded during that stay. A matched historical-specification refit on the revised primary complete-case population is provided as a model comparison.
Table 1 categories follow the HCUP NRD definitions for uniform discharge disposition, hospital teaching status, hospital ownership, hospital bed size, expected primary payer, and NCHS county urban–rural categories. In particular, HOSP_UR_TEACH codes 0, 1, and 2 mean metropolitan non-teaching, metropolitan teaching, and non-metropolitan hospital, respectively.
This model revision was made retrospectively before refitting outcome models and is not a pre-study prespecified analysis. Structural changes for empty or aliased terms, if any, followed the documented rules and did not use outcome significance or direction.
HF index admission and discharge. Demographics, hospital characteristics, year, index length of stay, discharge disposition, APR-DRG severity (including unclassified status), and individual legacy Elixhauser indicators precede the first-readmission destination. The revised primary model uses index-admission covariates with flexible age and index-length-of-stay terms. Claims-based severity and comorbidity flags can include conditions recorded during the index stay.
Interval before first readmission. Days from index discharge to first readmission occur before the readmission destination is known. Where included, this timing is distinguished from characteristics recorded during the first readmission.
First readmission. Diagnosis, severity, elective-status flags, hospital characteristics, and length of stay are concurrent with or follow destination selection. They are excluded from primary adjustment and considered separately only in supported sensitivity or secondary specifications.
After first-readmission discharge. The second readmission and its length of stay are post-exposure outcomes, not baseline confounders.
We use the annual NRD discharge weight, hospital as the primary sampling unit, and the year-specific NRD stratum. Year-specific identifiers are retained when pooling annual files. Survey-weighted logistic regression and design-based standardized predictive margins estimate the adjusted group risks and contrasts. The main effect measure is the risk difference (different minus same hospital), reported in percentage points with a 95% confidence interval. The risk ratio is secondary. Coefficients are reported on the scale used by the analysis output and are not interpreted as risk ratios. The supplement gives model convergence and rank, survey design degrees of freedom, fitted formula, spline knots, and alternate specifications.
The primary analysis is complete-case for model covariates. We report the analytic flow and covariate missingness by year and exposure group. No missing-category model was fitted. Complete-case analyses can be biased if covariate missingness is informative. The analysis plan and reporting checklist distinguish planned revision checks from post hoc decisions; this retrospective revision is not described as preregistered.


Ethics Funding and Author Information
Author confirmation required before submission: institutional review board determination and any waiver or exemption; applicable HCUP data-use compliance statement; author affiliations and contributions; funding and funder role; acknowledgments; and conflicts of interest. These details are intentionally not inferred from the analysis files.

The primary model is a survey-weighted logistic regression for the second-readmission outcome. In symbolic form, logit{Pr(Y = 1 | X)} = β₀ + Xβ; the exposure coefficient is on the log-odds scale. Adjusted risks are design-based predictive margins over the primary complete-case population, and the risk difference is the different-hospital margin minus the same-hospital margin. The model included hospital-switching exposure, year, sex, payer, ZIP income quartile, county urban–rural category, index-hospital bed size, urban-teaching status and ownership, natural spline terms for age and log(1 + index length of stay), index discharge disposition, APR-DRG severity, and estimable mapped legacy Elixhauser indicators. Full coefficient rows and the exact software formula are available in model_coefficients.csv and analysis_summary.csv.

title: Hospital switching at first readmission and recurrent hospitalization after heart failure
text:
Discussion

Principal findings
In 502,236 complete cases, adjusted 30-day risk was 31.44% (95% CI 31.26% to 31.61%) after a same-hospital first readmission and 32.49% (95% CI 32.18% to 32.80%) after a different-hospital first readmission. The adjusted risk difference was 1.06 percentage points (95% CI 0.71 to 1.40). This conditional association applies to people already selected by having a first readmission and surviving to its discharge.


Interpretation in context
Hospital switching is a descriptive site-of-care measure. It can represent a necessary transfer, emergency routing, patient preference, access constraints, insurance arrangements, or referral patterns. These data cannot separate those mechanisms or establish that switching itself is detrimental. Comparison with earlier HF fragmentation studies should emphasize differences in exposure, timing, and target population rather than claim that findings are directly contradictory or novel.


Limitations
Several limitations constrain interpretation. First, the cohort is conditioned on both a first readmission and survival to its discharge. Illness, access, care processes, and other factors may influence entry into this selected group and the subsequent outcome, creating selection bias. Second, administrative claims lack detailed physiologic severity, functional status, patient preference, distance, referral, ambulance routing, hospital capacity, and information exchange. Adjustment for measured baseline characteristics cannot remove residual confounding. Third, the hospital identifier identifies a site, not a care network or continuity of clinicians. Fourth, the diagnosis and transfer definitions are administrative algorithms without local clinical validation; transfer disposition can be imperfect. Fifth, follow-up cannot cross NRD year or state boundaries, and deaths outside the hospital are not observed. Finally, complete-case analyses can be biased if covariate missingness is informative; no missing-category sensitivity analysis was run.


Conclusions
Among adults with an eligible HF index admission who were readmitted within 30 days and discharged alive from that readmission, a different-hospital first readmission was associated with the subsequent 30-day inpatient admission risk estimated by the revised model. The result is specific to this selected survivor population and does not show that hospital switching causes, prevents, or is itself evidence of fragmented or lower-quality care.

Data access and reproducibility
The NRD is a restricted-use data product and person-level data cannot be redistributed. Researchers may obtain annual NRD files through HCUP subject to its data-use requirements. This project releases aggregate tables only after the project’s disclosure review. Raw NRD records, record-level linked cohorts, survey PSU frames, run manifests, private audit ledgers, and credentials are not part of the public release.
The analysis source is maintained separately from the public site. REPRODUCING.md documents the aggregate-only public render and the private full rebuild using authorized annual files. This report reads results from the certified aggregate CSV outputs in results/; it does not hard-code effect estimates. The current primary run is 20261024T035323+0500 and uses cohort run 20261023T191357+0500.
The public site provides the full 23-file disclosure-reviewed aggregate contract and the Word manuscript: cohort flow, crude weighted risks, adjusted risks (revised-run legacy filename), adjusted contrasts (revised-run legacy filename), Table 1, sensitivity results, E-value, subgroup results (empty in this run), main-model legacy output, conditional-model coefficients, missingness flow, complete-case flow, coarsened transfer exclusions, first-readmission mortality, secondary outcomes, utilization, cost availability, primary and matched-model risks, primary and matched-model contrasts, model coefficients, sensitivity risks, sensitivity contrasts, and analysis summary. The adjusted risks/contrasts and main-model legacy files are revised-run outputs, not historical model estimates. Private manifests, survey frames, record-level data, and audit files are not public.
